section: Creating a FASTA database from the command line
text:
Creating a FASTA database from the command line
prozor installs the script fgcz_create_fasta.R (it needs the docopt package). It reads all FASTA files and the annotation.txt in a directory, adds contaminants and reversed decoy sequences, and writes one FASTA file:
script=$(Rscript -e 'cat(system.file("script", "fgcz_create_fasta.R", package = "prozor"))')
Rscript "$script" -h
Rscript "$script" path/to/database_dir -o path/to/output_dir
Rscript "$script" path/to/database_dir nodecoy -c none -o path/to/output_dir

Result columns and list elements are snake_case too:

annotate_aho(), annotate_peptides(): protein_id, offset, protein_sequence, peptide_length, and peptide_seq for vector input (was proteinID, Offset, proteinSequence, lengthPeptide, peptideSeq)
compute_fdr(): fpr, simple_fdr, q_value_fpr, q_value_simple_fdr; compute_fdr_with_id() adds id (was FPR, SimpleFDR, qValue_FPR, qValue_SimpleFDR, ID)
greedy_to_table(): peptide, precursor_charge, protein (was Peptide, precursorCharge, Protein)
make_fasta_summary(as_string = FALSE): nr_sequences, length_summary, aa_freq; create_fgcz_fasta_db(): db, file_path, summary, call, db_name

predict_score_fdr(method = ) takes "simple_fdr" (default) or "fpr" (was "SimpleFDR", "FPR").
Default column names follow the results: annotate_peptides(peptide = "peptide_seq"), prepare_matrix(protein_id = "protein_id", peptide_id = "peptide_seq") (was "peptideSeq", "proteinID", "strippedSequence").
The data sets fdr_sample, protpepmetashort and pepprot have snake_case columns (protein_id, peptide_seq, peptide_mod_seq, precursor_charge, protein_length, peptide_length); bcd keeps COMET’s column names.
greedy(), last on CRAN in 0.3.1, has no alias; use greedy_parsimony().
write_fasta(fasta, file) takes one list of sequences, data first (was writeFasta(file, ...)); combine several lists with c().
Plots use ggplot2, which moved from Suggests to Imports. plot_fdr(), Cdsw$plot() and Cdsw$show_cycle() return ggplot objects and draw nothing themselves. The plot argument of Cdsw$sampling_breaks(), Cdsw$optimize_windows() and readjust_windows() is gone; use Cdsw$plot_breaks() and plot_windows().
annotate_peptides() sets matched for each occurrence of a peptide in a protein. It used to give every occurrence in a protein the same value, so a second, non-tryptic occurrence was flagged as tryptic.
annotate_aho() and annotate_peptides() stop for peptides with characters other than upper-case letters (AhoCorasickTrie 0.1.3 crashed R on them) and for duplicated protein names in fasta (they multiplied the result rows).
compute_fdr() and compute_fdr_with_id() rank decoys before targets within tied scores, so q-values no longer depend on the input order.
The default decoy pattern of compute_fdr_with_id() is "^REV_": only IDs starting with REV_ count as decoys. Pass decoy = "REV_" for the old matching anywhere in the ID.
predict_score_fdr() stops with an error when no score reaches the requested FDR, instead of returning Inf with a warning.
create_fgcz_fasta_db() requires output_dir (it used to write next to the database directory by default). inst/script/fgcz_create_fasta.R still writes next to the FASTA directory when -o is not given.
greedy_parsimony() no longer prints its run time.
prozor requires R 4.4.0 or later.





load_contaminants(set, no_human) loads any of the bundled contaminant sets.
plot_windows() shows the precursor masses with the DIA window boundaries; Cdsw$plot_breaks() compares the current breaks with equal-width and quantile breaks.





greedy_parsimony() assigns every peptide again. When several proteins tie, only those explaining exactly the same peptides are reported together ("A;B"); the others compete in later rounds. Since 2023 (GitHub only, not on CRAN), unrelated tied proteins were merged into one group and their remaining peptides were left without a protein.
greedy_to_table() works with modified peptides: the charge is taken after the last dot, so "AC[+57.0]K.2" gives peptide AC[+57.0]K and charge 2. Such names used to fail with “length of ‘dimnames’ [2] not equal to array extent”.
annotate_peptides() and prepare_matrix() accept tibbles; a tibble used to crash R or fail with “cannot xtfrm data frames”.
write_fasta() keeps a > inside a header (ADP>ATP used to become ADPATP).

A reference class that splits the MS1 mass range into windows with about equal numbers of precursors, subject to minimum and maximum window widths.

breaks


The window boundaries.

digits

Repeatedly assigns all unexplained peptides of the protein that explains the most of them. Proteins that explain exactly the same peptides are reported together, separated by ;.



greedy_parsimony(pepprot)







pepprot


A peptide-by-protein matrix, as returned by prepare_matrix().






A named list with one element per peptide (row of pepprot): the protein, or ;-separated protein group, it is assigned to.



Other protein inference: annotate_aho(), annotate_peptides(), greedy_to_table(), prepare_matrix()




library("prozor")

data(protpepmetashort)
pepprot <- prepare_matrix(protpepmetashort, peptide_id = "peptide_mod_seq")
groups <- greedy_parsimony(pepprot)
# every precursor is assigned to exactly one protein group

text:
Finds every occurrence of each peptide in fasta with annotate_aho() and flags whether it is a tryptic match. Peptides that occur in no protein are dropped.



annotate_peptides(
  pepinfo,
  fasta,
  peptide = "peptide_seq",
  prefix = "(([RK])|(^)|(^M))",
  suffix = ""
)







pepinfo


A character vector of peptide sequences, or a data frame (or tibble) with the column peptide and any further columns, such as the charge state, which are kept.




fasta


A list of protein sequences with unique names, as returned by read_peptide_fasta().




peptide


Name of the column with the peptide sequences.




prefix


Regular expression the residues before a match must end with.




suffix


Regular expression the residues after a match must start with.






Each occurrence of a peptide in a protein is one row. matched is TRUE when the residues before that occurrence match prefix and the residues after it match suffix; by default, when the occurrence follows K or R, starts the protein, or follows its initial methionine.



A data frame with one row per row of pepinfo and protein occurrence: the columns of pepinfo, protein_id, offset (1-based start of the peptide), protein_sequence, matched and peptide_length. NULL, with a warning, if no peptide occurs in fasta.



Other protein inference: annotate_aho(), greedy_parsimony(), greedy_to_table(), prepare_matrix()




library("prozor")

file <- system.file("extdata/IDResults.txt.gz", package = "prozor")
peptides <- unique(utils::read.delim(file)$peptideSeq)
fasta_file <- system.file("p1000_db1_example/Annotation_canSeq.fasta.gz", package = "prozor")
fasta <- read_peptide_fasta(fasta_file)
annot <- annotate_peptides(peptides[1:20], fasta)

title: Target Decoy FDR
text: Here we describe how you can estimate the false discovery rate (FDR) when matching your spectra against a FASTA sequence database using spectra search engines such as Mascot or Comet. The sequence database contains forward sequences and the same number of reverse sequences.

title: Target Decoy FDR
text:
The data
The data needs to have two columns, one with a label, to distinguish targets and decoys, the other with a score. Then you also need to know if a larger score or a smaller score is better. In our example data, we have two scores: score and score2. While the score is better if it is smaller (e.g., posterior error probability), score2 is better if it is larger.

title: Target Decoy FDR
text:
Types of FDR
We define
 * false positives (FP) as the number of passing decoy assignments
 * true positives (TP) as the number of passing forward hits.

False positive rate
Which is the “Fraction of incorrect assignments above score threshold”. The multiplier 2 is needed here since we assume that also the forward sequences have false assignments.
\[
FPR = \frac{2 \cdot FP}{TP + FP}
\]
This is taken from the reference by (Elias and Gygi 2007). (Storey and Tibshirani 2003) defines FPR differently. Kaell points out that the FPR here actually should be named FDR and that “Many proteomics papers incorrectly refer to this quantity as the false positive rate.”


Simple FDR
“The FDR associated with a particular score threshold is defined as the expected percentage of accepted PSMs that are incorrect, where an accepted PSM is one that scores above the threshold (Many proteomics papers incorrectly refer to this quantity as the false positive rate).” ((Käll et al. 2007))
The Simple FDR introduced by ((Käll et al. 2007)) is defined by :
\[
SimpleFDR =  \frac{FP}{TP}
\]
“For a given score threshold, we count the number of decoy PSMs above the threshold and the number of target PSMs above the threshold. We can now estimate the FDR by simply computing the ratio of these two values (SimpleFDR).”(Käll et al. 2007)

fdr_curves <- data.frame(
  score = rep(fdr1$score, 2),
  fdr = 100 * c(fdr1$simple_fdr, fdr1$q_value_simple_fdr),
  curve = rep(c("SimpleFDR", "q-value"), each = length(fdr1$score))
)
ggplot(fdr_curves, aes(x = score, y = fdr, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.002), ylim = c(0, 0.05)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(SimpleFDR = "black", "q-value" = "#E69F00")) +
  labs(x = "score (smaller is better)", y = "FDR (%)", colour = NULL)








Although the score is getting better (smaller) the FDR may increase since the number of TP in the denominator decreases while the number of FP stays the same. Therefore Storey and Tibshirani proposed the q-value, “which in our case is defined as the minimal FDR threshold at which a given PSM is accepted”(Käll et al. 2007).
